summary:
Anita (Vellum) presents a TDD framework for building reliable agentic AI workflows. She contextualizes the field's evolution: 2023's AI wrappers lacked defensibility, while Cursor AI reached $100M ARR in 12 months through orchestration, not just better models. After GPT-4, model improvements slowed, but DeepSeek R1's reinforcement learning without labeled data and reasoning models using Chain of Thought reopened progress. Traditional benchmarks are saturated; new ones like Humanities Last Exam show even frontier models struggle.

The TDD lifecycle has four stages. Experimentation involves trying prompting techniques, engaging domain experts, and staying model-agnostic. Evaluation requires datasets of hundreds of examples, balancing quality/cost/latency/privacy, using ground-truth or LLM-as-judge, custom metrics, and guardrails at internal nodes. Production deployment demands logging all LLM calls, handling API reliability with retries and fallbacks, version control, staging, decoupling AI from app releases, caching for repeat queries, and eventually fine-tuning custom models from production data.

For agentic workflows, evaluation must assess agent behavior—not just performance—ensuring agents make correct decisions and follow intended logic. Anita introduces a five-level agentic behavior framework: L0 (basic LLM call with vector DB retrieval), L1 (tool use with model-decided API calls, memory, parallel execution—production-ready today, citing Vellum clients like Redfin and Headspace), L2 (structured reasoning with planning, task breakdown, and self-evaluation loops—where most innovation is expected this year), L3 (autonomous agents that stay alive and act proactively), and L4 (fully creative systems—currently out of reach due to overfitting and inductive bias).

She demos an SEO agent operating between L1 and L2. An SEO analyst takes a keyword plus parameters like writing style and audience, calls Google search, and analyzes top-ranking articles to identify strengths to reinforce and gaps to fill. A researcher captures additional data on missing pieces. A writer drafts using all gathered context—not generic output but grounded content, optionally connected to a RAG database. An LLM-based editor evaluates the draft against predefined rules, feeding feedback through a memory component (chat history between writer and editor) in a continuous loop. The loop breaks when the evaluator rates the post excellent or after a minimum iteration count. The demo produced a developer guide on Chain of Thought prompting with ~118-second latency (typically 300 seconds with more loops). Anita concludes by announcing Vellum's open-source workflow SDK, offering infinitely customizable, self-documenting syntax with UI-code sync, designed to bridge product and engineering teams while maintaining the TDD approach.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.summary: Anita introduces herself and Vellum's work with hundreds of companies. She notes that teams adopting TDD built stronger production AI. She contextualizes the field: 2023 was dominated by AI wrappers with no defensibility, while today Cursor AI reached $100M ARR in 12 months thanks to better orchestration patterns, not just better models.

sections.title: Model Evolution and New Training Methods
sections.summary: Model improvements slowed after GPT-4 as scaling data hit diminishing returns. Recently, DeepSeek R1 introduced pure reinforcement learning without labeled data, and reasoning models use Chain of Thought at inference time. New benchmarks like Humanities Last Exam show even frontier models struggle with truly difficult tasks.

sections.title: Evolution of AI Orchestration Techniques
sections.summary: Techniques evolved in parallel to model training: better prompting, Chain of Thought, RAG for grounding, memory for multi-threaded conversations, long context, graph RAG, reasoning models, and agentic RAG. But techniques alone are insufficient—teams must deeply understand their problem and adopt TDD.

sections.title: TDD Lifecycle and Experimentation Stage
sections.summary: The best AI teams follow: experiment, evaluate, scale, deploy, and continuously monitor. During experimentation, try different prompting techniques (few-shot, CoT, prompt chaining, ReAct), involve domain experts rather than engineers, and stay model-agnostic.

sections.title: Evaluation Stage
sections.summary: Create datasets of hundreds of examples. Balance quality, cost, latency, and privacy with explicit tradeoffs. Use ground-truth data or LLM-as-judge. Use flexible testing frameworks with custom metrics in Python or TypeScript, run guardrails at internal nodes, and evaluate at every stage.

sections.title: Production Deployment, Caching, and Fine-tuning
sections.summary: Log all LLM calls, inputs, outputs, and latency. Handle API reliability with retries and fallbacks. Use version control and staging. Decouple AI deployments from app releases. Build a caching layer to reduce costs and latency for repeat queries. Once stable in production, use accumulated data to fine-tune custom models. For agentic workflows, evaluation must also assess agent behavior—ensuring correct decisions and intended logic—not just performance metrics.

sections.title: Five Levels of Agentic Behavior (L0–L4)
sections.summary: Anita defines a framework of five agentic behavior levels. L0: basic LLM call with vector DB retrieval and inline evals; reasoning is baked into the prompt with no external orchestration. L1: tool use—the model decides when to call APIs or query the vector DB; memory supports multi-threaded conversations; execution can be parallel; evaluation needed at every step. L2: structured reasoning—workflow can trigger, plan actions, break down tasks, evaluate usefulness, and loop until complete, but the process is finite. L3: autonomy—agent stays alive, monitors environments (email, Slack, Google Drive), and proactively acts or requests human input. L4: fully creative—invents new workflows, tools, and agents; currently out of reach due to overfitting and inductive bias in models.

sections.title: Current State of Agentic AI
sections.summary: L1 is where production-grade solutions exist today; Vellum clients like Redfin, DRA, and Headspace operate at this level, focusing on orchestration, data integration, and continuous TDD-driven improvement. L2 is where Anita expects most innovation this year, with agents planning and reasoning using models like o1, o3, or DeepSeek. L3 and L4 remain limited by current models and surrounding logic. Anita directs attendees to a downloadable resource with architectures, testing stages, and expert insights.

sections.title: SEO Agent Demo
sections.summary: Anita demos her SEO agent (L1–L2) automating keyword research, content analysis, and content creation. The SEO analyst takes a keyword plus writing style and audience parameters, calls Google search, and analyzes top-ranking articles to identify strengths to reinforce and gaps to fill. A researcher captures additional data on missing pieces. A writer drafts using all gathered context—grounded, not generic output—optionally connected to a RAG database. An LLM-based editor evaluates the draft against predefined rules, feeding feedback through a memory component (chat history between writer and editor) in a continuous loop. The loop breaks when the evaluator rates the post excellent (rarely happens) or after a minimum iteration count. The demo produced a developer guide on Chain of Thought prompting with ~118-second latency (typically 300 seconds with more loops).

sections.title: Vellum Workflow SDK Announcement and Closing
sections.summary: Anita introduces Vellum Workflows, designed to bridge product and engineering teams for faster AI development while following the TDD approach. She announces a new open-source, free workflow SDK providing infinitely customizable building blocks with a self-documenting, expressive syntax that shows how agents work directly in code. The UI and code stay in sync so teams stay aligned during definition, debugging, and improvement. She shares a GitHub QR code for the repo and closes by inviting attendees to connect on LinkedIn, email, or Twitter for further AI discussions.

limitations: Hallucinations remain a problem in model outputs.
Overfitting remains a problem; models favor their training data.
Model performance improvements slowed after GPT-4; big jumps are no longer guaranteed by scaling data.
Traditional benchmarks are saturated and do not adequately capture reasoning model performance.
No AI system perfectly optimizes quality, cost, latency, and privacy simultaneously—tradeoffs are required.
L4 (fully creative AI) is out of reach due to overfitting and inductive bias in current models.
L3 and L4 agentic levels are limited by current model capabilities and surrounding logic.
The SEO agent's evaluator rarely rates output as 'excellent,' so the feedback loop requires a minimum iteration count to break.
